title: Maths Area
strapline: Counting, comparing, patterning — number as something you play with, not something you're tested on.
intent: Children build a secure feel for small numbers: counting with one-to-one correspondence, knowing the last number tells you how many, seeing two or three at a glance.
Children sort, match and classify by rules that matter to them — and can tell you the rule.
Children copy, continue and create patterns, and start predicting what comes next.
Children compare and measure through their hands: heavier, longer, full, more, not enough.
Children use maths to solve problems that are genuinely theirs — sharing the snack, needing one more chair, whose tower is tallest.
implementation: Stock countable things worth counting: conkers, buttons, gems, shells — loose parts with texture and appeal, in quantities that allow big collections.
Count aloud slowly with a finger-touch per object, and make a fuss of the last number: 'one, two, three, FOUR — four conkers!'
Make deliberate mistakes for children to catch — count an object twice, skip one, declare the wrong total.
Provide five-frames, tens-frames and dice patterns casually alongside the loose parts, so subitising happens through play, not drill.
Feed in comparing language at the balance scales — heavier, lighter, balanced — and let children test their guesses.
Start a pattern with beads or pebbles and leave it unfinished where a child will find it.
Weave maths into real jobs all day — cups at snack, names at register, steps on the stairs — so the maths area is a hub, not a fence.
key_questions: How many do you think there are — shall we check?
How did you decide which ones go together?
What comes next in your pattern? How do you know?
Which is heavier — and what if we add one more?
Have we got enough for everyone? How could we find out?

impact.text: Children sort collections by their own rule — all the shiny ones, all the tiny ones — and explain the rule when asked.
Children count small groups accurately, touching one object per number word, and know the last number is the answer.
Children glance at a dice face or a small handful and say 'three!' without counting.
Children copy, continue and invent their own repeating patterns with beads and pebbles, and talk through what comes next.
Children compare amounts and weights at the scales using words like heavier, longer, more, not many.
Children reach for maths unprompted to solve real problems — dealing out the snack fairly, fetching one more cup.
Children stick at a tricky maths challenge — balancing the scales exactly, finishing a long pattern — until they feel the win.

enhancements: A mystery bag of conkers each morning — grab a handful, estimate, then count to check.
Balance scales with natural treasures: how many acorns weigh the same as one fir cone?
Number hunt cards for the room and garden — find three of something, find the numeral 5 hiding somewhere.
Birthday-candle counting: playdough cakes needing exactly the right number of candles for each cuddly toy's age.
A washing line of numbered socks that keeps getting pegged up in the wrong order overnight.
Big floor dice and giant dominoes for whole-body subitising games.
A 'how many sleeps' calendar for something the children are genuinely waiting for.

playing_exploring: Children handle beautiful countable things because they want to — the maths follows the fascination.
Open-ended collections invite children to invent their own sorting games and rules.
active_learning: Checking a guess by counting — and being right — delivers a satisfaction children chase again.
Children persist to balance the scales or complete the pattern exactly.
creating_thinking: Children spot patterns and use them to predict, the root of mathematical thinking.
They find their own strategies — grouping, lining up, using fingers — and can say what worked.
